title: MedSAD-Clip: Supervised Clip with Token-Patch Cross-Attention for Medical Anomaly Detection and Segmentation
text: Unlike existing work using dot-product heatmaps directly as masks, TPCA forms token-conditioned features and concatenates them with rich image features before decoding, injecting granular language cues while preserving visual detail and sharpening lesion boundaries. Secondly, we integrate multilevel image adapters and a learnable text prompt module into the pretrained CLIP [17, 46]. Image adapters transfer general-domain representations to medical imaging, while the learnable prompt module further facilitates adaptation to various clinical contexts, anatomical regions, and imaging modalities. Lastly, we propose Margin-based imagetext Contrastive Loss (MC-Loss), which explicitly enforces a larger semantic distance between normal and abnormal image-text pairs, guiding the model to learn a discriminative boundary and thereby improving image-level anomaly detection.

title: MedSAD-Clip: Supervised Clip with Token-Patch Cross-Attention for Medical Anomaly Detection and Segmentation
text: The model extends CLIP [30] with adapter modules and learnable prompts to adapt to medical image analysis. medical anomaly detection tasks. For example, MVFA [17], Aa-CLIP [27], and Fe-CLIP [11] leverage vision adapters to transfer knowledge from the general domain to the medical domain, enabling more effective learning of domain-specific visual representations for accurate detection of medical anomalies. However, these models rely on fixed, handcrafted prompts to represent medical concepts, limiting adaptability to diverse imaging contexts and textual variations. MediCLIP [46], AnomalyCLIP [49], and MadCLIP [36] further extend this paradigm by introducing learnable prompt representations that enhance cross-modal alignment and better capture semantic variations in medical anomaly detection.

title: MedSAD-Clip: Supervised Clip with Token-Patch Cross-Attention for Medical Anomaly Detection and Segmentation
text: We build upon the CLIP framework [30], which aligns image and text representations through a Vision Transformer and Text Transformer. To adapt to medical domain, we introduce adapter modules, inspired by the MVFA model [17], to extract domainspecific semantic features, and learnable prompt embeddings, following the prompt-learning strategy in [46], to adaptively generalize across various medical anomaly detection tasks. Specifically, after passing the image through CLIP Vision Transformer, our framework incorporates two dedicated adapters: the DetAdapter for classification and the SegAdapter for segmentation. In parallel, the learnable text prompt is fed into the Text Transformer to obtain text embedding.

To improve their adaptability, we append a set of K learnable tokens {p1, p2, . . . , pK} to the end of each anchor prompt, forming the learnable prompt representations: ˜Tnorm = [Tnorm, p1, . . . , pK], (6) ˜Tabn = [Tabn, p1, . . . , pK]. This design allows the model to automatically adjust to different organs or disease contexts without manually crafting diverse prompt templates. Then, we encode them through the CLIP text encoder to obtain semantic text embeddings: Ft = TextEncoder([ ˜Tnorm, ˜Tabn]), (8) where Ft ∈R2×Nt×D denotes the dual text feature representation for the normal and abnormal descriptions, and D is the embedding dimension of the shared CLIP space, Nt denotes the fixed length of the prompt.

title: MedSAD-Clip: Supervised Clip with Token-Patch Cross-Attention for Medical Anomaly Detection and Segmentation
text: In this section, we introduce a Token-Patch Cross-Attention (TPCA) module, inspired by recent vision–language interaction methods [43]. Unlike existing CLIP-based anomaly detection models that employ simple fusion techniques such as concatenation [17, 19, 39, 46] or average aggregation [5] before generating the anomaly map, our TPCA explicitly models the fine-grained correspondence between textual semantics and localized image regions. Using cross-attention, we obtain token-conditioned feature maps, which are then fused with the original image representations before decoding. This integration retains low-level structural detail while introducing fine-grained, token-level semantics as complementary guidance.

title: MADPOT: Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP Adaptation and Partial Optimal Transport
text: Medical anomaly detection (AD) aims to identify unusual patterns in medical data, a task made challenging by the absence of a universal definition of anomaly and the considerable variability in medical images, both across different modalities and anatomical regions [10,19,40]. Ideally, a model should exhibit versatility across diverse data types, regardless of variations in anomaly size, modality, or underlying anatomical structures. Additionally, it should be capable of handling tasks involving few-shot learning (where only a limited number of labeled examples are available for training, e.g., [12,18]) or zero-shot learning (where the model is trained on one set of modalities but tested on completely unseen modalities, e.g., [19]).

title: MADPOT: Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP Adaptation and Partial Optimal Transport
text: Our method, called MADPOT, demonstrates superior performance in medical AD across few-shot, zero-shot, and cross-dataset settings (i.e., training and testing occur on the same modality but different datasets), surpassing all stateof-the-art (SOTA) methods. Additionally, our pipeline eliminates the need for memory banks, as seen in e.g., [19], or additional synthetic data, as used in [41]. The main contributions of our work are: (1) The pioneering investigation of prompt learning with OT and POT and their novel integration with CL in medical AD, particularly in few-shot and zeroshot settings. This is the first exploration of these techniques in this context, highlighting their potential for reducing data dependency and enhancing model flexibility. (2) A comprehensive evaluation of OT, POT, CL, and vision adapters, alongside their various combinations, providing an in-depth analysis of how these components contribute to model performance across datasets with substantial modality and distribution differences. (3) Demonstration of strong generalization and noticeable performance improvements, validated through cross-dataset and cross-modality evaluations.

title: MADPOT: Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP Adaptation and Partial Optimal Transport
text: April-GAN [10] maps CLIPextracted visual features to the text feature space and uses multiple memory banks, which is an expensive setup with limited generalization. In medical AD, MVFA [19] extends this by applying multi-level CLIP adaptation with fixed prompts. MediCLIP [41], instead, uses learnable prompts [42] and synthetic abnormal data to improve generalization. However, a learnable prompt with OT/POT, as shown in our experiments, hinders performance, especially in certain modalities (e.g., histopathology).

title: MADPOT: Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP Adaptation and Partial Optimal Transport
text: To adapt the pre-trained CLIP vision encoder [30] for the AC and AS tasks in medical imaging, MADPOT uses adapter and projection layers. This approach follows the findings of [19], which shows that it is preferable to traditional fine-tuning, as it helps avoid overfitting due to high model complexity and limited data. We append a small set of learnable layers to the visual branches of CLIP while keeping the backbone frozen. In detail, for an input image x, we extract the i-th layer feature from the CLIP vision encoder, denoted as f i vis(x) ∈RG×d.

title: MADPOT: Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP Adaptation and Partial Optimal Transport
text: We used the BMAD benchmark [3] in line with the latest SOTA: MVFA [19]. It consists of five modalities and six datasets: brain MRI [1,2,28], liver CT [6,25], chest X-ray [37], retinal OCT (composed of two datasets; OCT17 [22], and RESC [17]), and digital histopathology (HIS) [4]. Brain, Liver, and RESC supply annotations for both AC and AS, while OCT17, Chest, and HIS are relevant only for AC.

title: MADPOT: Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP Adaptation and Partial Optimal Transport
text: Implementation Details. We use the CLIP [30] with the ViT-L/14 backbone in line with the recent SOTA, such as [10,19,41]. This CLIP model consists of 24 layers. We insert an adapter at the 12th layer and attach the projector to the 24th layer.

title: MADPOT: Medical Anomaly Detection with CLIP Adaptation and Partial Optimal Transport
text: We insert an adapter at the 12th layer and attach the projector to the 24th layer. This configuration is motivated by the ablation study in MVFA [19], which shows that using the 12th layer yields better performance compared to alternatives such as the 6th, 18th, or their combinations. The number of prompts in a prompt set is fixed to 4 as in PLOT [9]. Training is performed with the Adam optimizer with the learning rate of 1e−3, batch size 16, for 100 epochs.

text: Despite this advancement, the method falls short in identifying and localizing lesion areas. Recent studies [28,8,7,10] have applied CLIP [19] for zero-/few-shot anomaly detection with impressive performance. However, these methods require an auxiliary dataset with real anomaly images and corresponding pixel-level anomaly labels for model training, which is often challenging to obtain in the medical field. To address this limitation, we propose MediCLIP, which employs synthetic anomaly images for model training instead of relying on an auxiliary dataset.

title: FiLo++: Zero-/Few-Shot Anomaly Detection by Fused Fine-Grained Descriptions and Deformable Localization
text: For localization, existing ZSAD methods typically compare image patches directly with text features, resulting in false positives in background regions. Our DefLoc method effectively eliminates background areas and improves localization accuracy by employing Grounding DINO, position-enhanced text descriptions, and the MDCI module. identifying lesions in medical contexts [6], [7], and monitoring abnormal behaviors of vehicles and pedestrians in transportation [8]–[11]. Traditional anomaly detection methods [12]– [14] typically regard the problem as one-class classification, where the model is trained on a large number of normal samples and subsequently attempts to detect out-of-distribution anomalies. Although these methods perform well, they lose effectiveness in scenarios where large-scale normal data collection is challenging (e.g., cold-start settings).

title: Exploring Intrinsic Normal Prototypes within a Single Image for Universal Anomaly Detection
text: Unsupervised image anomaly detection (AD) [4, 43] seeks to identify abnormal patterns in images and localize anomalous regions by learning solely from normal samples. This technique has seen widespread application in industrial defect detection [2, 51] and medical disease screening [22]. Recently, various specialized tasks have emerged in response to real-world demands, from conventional singleclass AD [32, 38] to more advanced few-shot AD [20, 25] and multi-class AD [17, 44, 46]. Although the composition of normal samples varies across these tasks, the fundamental principle remains unchanged: modeling normality in the training data and assessing whether a test image aligns with this learned normality.

title: Co-Progression Knowledge Distillation with Knowledge Prototype for Industrial Anomaly Detection
text: Unsupervised anomaly detection is a critical task in computer vision, with applications in industrial quality control(Roth et al. 2022) and medical imaging(Huang et al. 2024). The goal is to identify abnormal patterns in images without relying on pre-labeled defective samples. This approach has gained significant traction in domains where data collection is challenging, such as industrial defect detection and medical imaging.
